findings.title: A gap (suspend, stall, forward clock step) is stored as an ordinary workload row and rolled up as observed zero-use time
findings.evidence: Code: sampler.py:59 gives a gap batch interval_s=max(elapsed, wall) (the whole gap) with zero deltas; rules.py:219-221 copies interval_s into every WorkloadSample; WorkloadSample has no gap field (models.py:135-147); raw.py:102-129 writes system_raw and workload_raw rows whatever batch.gap says; rollup.py:53,60,68-71 add the interval to covered_s, the memory mean and both histograms. Probe: .venv/bin/python docs/review/probes/c-storage/gap_in_rollup.py (2 cores busy for 10 min, 1 h asleep, 10 min busy): 'workload_raw row at 10:10:01.00: interval_s 3601, cpu_s 0.0, memory 50 MiB <- the gap, stored as an ordinary sample'; 'minute bucket 09:40:00.00: covered_s 3601 of 60, samples 1, cpu_s 0, seconds in the lowest cores bin (under 0.01 cores) 3601'; 'hour 09:00: covered_s 4201, cpu_s/covered_s 0.29 cores, p50 0.006, p95 2.08, well_covered True' (true: 2.00 cores, 600 s observed, so it should NOT be well covered); 'system_raw ... busy share 12.5% (true while observed: 50.0%)'.
findings.impact: Breaks the stated rule 'covered seconds and sample count, so a gap is never read as zero use' (docs/06-storage.md:38, docs/17-build-prompt.md:120). After every laptop sleep, mean CPU, the memory mean and p50/p95 of the bucket that holds the gap's midpoint (30 minutes before wake for a 1 h sleep) are dragged towards zero. A minute bucket claims 3601 covered seconds out of 60, and the hour passes well_covered, so it feeds baselines and trends. The system busy share is quartered. Every overnight sleep therefore puts a false idle stretch into the baseline and trend data.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/raw.py RawFile.write: when batch.gap is true, write the gap row and write the workload_raw and system_raw rows with interval_s 0. roll_up already skips interval_s <= 0 (rollup.py:50), and the memory gauge at wake is kept. Or drop those rows. src/submeter/store/rollup.py SeriesAccumulator.add: refuse (raise) a sample with interval_s greater than width_s, so the case cannot pass silently. Add a test that follows a suspend from Sampler to a bucket and asserts covered_s <= width_s and well_covered False.
findings.cost: About 6 changed lines in raw.py and rollup.py, plus one test.
findings.refutation_attempt: Searched docs and src for 'gap'. docs/14-baseline-modules.md:298 says only that a gap batch's process rows are written in full. Nothing says workload rows are suppressed. R08 and R24 claim this case is fixed. Re-ran the probe and got the same output. b-measurement/gap_rule.out.txt part 2 also shows aggregate() returning a 3601 s workload row, so another lens confirms the first half. The bucket consequences are measured only here.

findings.title: Allowed sampling settings turn every sample into a gap that discards its CPU, and samples of 60 s or more break minute buckets and their 30-second finality
findings.evidence: docs/08-configuration.md:62-63,71 allow idle_interval up to 60 s, cold_interval up to 60 s and on_battery_multiplier up to 10. sampler.py:39,55 has a fixed gap_after_s=30. Probe long_intervals.py part 1: 'cold_interval 60s accepted; 60 s between samples: 20 of 20 batches are gaps, CPU kept 0 of 600 s'; 'idle_interval 20s, on_battery_multiplier 2 accepted; 40 s ... CPU kept 0 of 400 s'; 'idle 60s x battery 10 ... CPU kept 0 of 6000 s'. Part 3, with the threshold lifted: '120 s samples: 30 minute buckets exist in the hour, covered_s 120 to 120 of 60, well covered 30; a sample is written up to 59 s after its bucket ended (a bucket is final after 30 s)'; '600 s samples: ... covered_s 600 of 60 ... up to 299 s after'. docs/17-build-prompt.md:123: 'A bucket is final 30 seconds after it ends.'
findings.impact: On battery, or with any allowed idle or cold interval over 30 s, CPU totals for every workload drop to zero while the machine is busy. That is a wrong cost figure, not a missing one. Once the threshold is fixed, a single long sample still lands whole in one minute (twice the bucket's width), leaves its neighbours empty, and arrives after that minute is final, so an idempotent roll-up that honours finality never sees it.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/collector/sampler.py: derive the gap threshold from the interval in force: gap when elapsed exceeds max(30 s, 3 x the expected interval) or wall - elapsed exceeds the slack. docs/14-baseline-modules.md:244 should state that rule. src/submeter/store/rollup.py roll_up: split a sample that spans bucket edges pro rata by time, giving counters by share and gauges by weight. docs/17-build-prompt.md:123: 'a bucket is final 30 seconds after it ends, or one longest interval after it ends if that is later'.
findings.cost: About 25 lines across sampler.py and rollup.py, a sentence in each of two docs, and tests.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether config validation forbids these combinations. load_settings accepted every one, as the probe printed 'accepted'. Checked docs/08 for a stated gap rule: none, and docs/14:244 states the fixed 30 s. The same threshold result is in b-measurement/gap_rule.out.txt part 1. The bucket and finality half is new here.

findings.title: The window query and the roll-up assign samples to buckets by different rules, so minute buckets filled by time-window queries lose or misplace CPU
findings.evidence: raw.py:199 selects by sample END ('WHERE ts > ? AND ts <= ?'). rollup.py:110 assigns by MIDDLE (taken_at - interval_s/2). Probe bucket_membership.py, one hour at 1 CPU-s/s: interval 1 s, first tick 0.37 s after the minute: 'A window query, roll_up, keep the asked bucket cpu 3540.0 of 3600.0 (-1.67%)'; 'B ... upsert every bucket cpu 118.0 of 3600.0 (-96.72%)'; 'C one accumulator per bucket 3600.0 (+0.00%)'. Interval 5 s: A -8.33%, B -90.28%. Interval 10 s: A -16.67%, B -82.22%. 'the 09:01 window alone gives a bucket at 09:00:00.00 with 1 samples'. Midnight: 'file 2026-11-21: sample ending day+1 00:00:00.37 -> roll_up bucket 23:59:00.00; inside the 23:59 window query: False'.
findings.impact: The phase 1 gate 'CPU-hours from the hourly tier match the raw sum within 0.1%' (docs/15-phases-and-decisions.md:13) fails under the obvious server implementation, and the tests miss it because they use whole-second timestamps. Approach B, an idempotent upsert of whatever roll_up returns, overwrites good buckets with one-sample fragments. Samples just after UTC midnight belong to a bucket of the previous day but live in the next day's file.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/rollup.py: one membership rule that matches the query. Either assign by end, with the bucket being the half-open (start, start+width] that holds taken_at, as workload_samples already selects, or take the bucket window from the caller and split by time as in the previous finding. docs/17-build-prompt.md Store: 'a sample belongs to the bucket that holds its end; the roll-up of a bucket near UTC midnight reads both day files'. Add a test with fractional timestamps (phase 0.37) through workload_samples and roll_up.
findings.cost: About 5 lines in rollup.py, one sentence in the doc, and one test.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked for a writer that fixes the convention: none exists yet (docs/14: 'The writers for the minute and history files are still to build'). Approach C is exact, so a careful builder could avoid the loss, but nothing in the brief tells them to, and roll_up's own docstring invites A and B. b-measurement/rollup_conventions.out.txt reports the same rule mismatch at the hourly tier ('worst 18.698%' at 60 s). The minute-pipeline and midnight-file figures are new here.

findings.title: A wall clock stepped backwards silently overwrites stored samples, reopens a closed day file and delays keyframes
findings.evidence: sampler.py:55 marks a gap only when wall runs AHEAD of monotonic. raw.py:103,113,175 use INSERT OR REPLACE keyed on ts. raw.py:265-274 reopens any day that differs from the current one. Probe clock_steps.py (one core busy, synthetic clocks): '2. stepped backwards 30 s, whole-second ticks: 120 batches written, true CPU 120 s / 90 workload rows, CPU 90 s ... gap rows 0'; '2b ... the minute 12:00:00.00 holds 90 covered seconds and 90 CPU-s; event rows that mark the step: 0'; '3. stepped backwards 50 s across UTC midnight: 2026-11-20.db CPU 39 s; 2026-11-21.db CPU 31 s; files written, in order: 2026-11-20.db x39, 2026-11-21.db x20, 2026-11-20.db x30, 2026-11-21.db x31'; '4. stepped backwards 3600 s ... keyframes at ticks [1, 601, 4801]; the longest wait between two is 4200 s'; '5. a process born 0.6 s before the first sample after a step back used 0.5 CPU-s; the sampler credits it 0.0 s'.
findings.impact: A step back loses CPU with no trace: 30 of 120 CPU-s, or 50 of 120 across midnight. Where no rows collide, it packs more than 60 covered seconds into a minute. It breaks 'A closed day's file is never written again' (docs/17-build-prompt.md:112) and R31's promise that no query looks back more than 10 minutes. Nothing records the step, so no epoch or chart mark explains the dip. The code behaviour is verified. How often Windows steps the clock back is not.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/collector/sampler.py: when elapsed - wall exceeds the slack, the wall clock went back. Record a 'clock stepped' event, and set taken_at = previous.taken_at + elapsed until the wall clock catches up, so stored time never decreases. src/submeter/store/raw.py: plain INSERT on workload_raw, system_raw and process_raw, so a duplicate key raises instead of overwriting. RawStore.write never reopens a day earlier than the current file. docs/14-baseline-modules.md:244: state the backward-step rule.
findings.cost: About 15 lines in sampler.py and raw.py, and two tests.
findings.refutation_attempt: Looked for handling of backward steps in docs/05, 06, 14 and 17, and in docs/reference/windows-priorities.md section 5 (forward steps and suspend only). R08 covers sleep, not backward steps. Re-ran the probe with a 30.25 s step to rule out a whole-second artefact: no rows were lost, but the double-counted minute remains.

findings.title: Nothing records what has been rolled up, so retention can delete raw data that was never rolled up, and with the server stopped nothing enforces retention at all
findings.evidence: files.py:121-131: expired_raw tests only the file's age. Probe retention_calendar.py part 4: 'server back at 09:00 on the 15th after five days away: expired_raw offers ['2026-11-10.db', '2026-11-11.db', '2026-11-12.db'] for deletion. FileMap members that record what has been rolled up: none. Raw files on disk while it was away: 6, with nothing deleting them'. docs/17-build-prompt.md:53 gives retention to the server ('rollups, retention'), docs/06-storage.md:9 says 'Each program writes only its own files', and docs/17-build-prompt.md:123 says 'Build hourly buckets from raw data while it still exists'. No doc says who deletes raw files or in which order catch-up and retention run (grep for 'delet', 'catch up', 'rolled up', 'not running': nothing).
findings.impact: If the server is down for more than 48 hours while the collector runs (crash, not installed as a task, the user stops it), then on restart a retention pass that runs before catch-up deletes days whose minute and hourly buckets were never built. That trend and history data is lost for good. While the server is down, the 2 GB budget is not enforced on the collector's growing raw files.
findings.proposed_change: docs/06-storage.md and docs/17-build-prompt.md Store: 'The server keeps a rolled-up-until mark in the history file. At start it rolls up every raw day it holds, oldest first, before any retention pass, and it deletes a raw file only once the mark has passed that day's end.' Name who deletes raw files. src/submeter/store/files.py expired_raw: take the mark as an argument and never return a day after it.
findings.cost: Two sentences in each doc, and about 5 lines in files.py.
findings.decision_question: Who deletes raw files: only the server, gated on the rolled-up-until mark, or the server normally plus a collector-side safety cap (for example delete raw files older than 7 days, or above 1.5 x the budget) so a dead server cannot fill the disk? Recommendation: the server deletes, gated on the mark, and the collector applies only a hard safety cap with a logged finding.
findings.refutation_attempt: Searched every doc for a catch-up or watermark rule and for who deletes: none. R23 and R26 cover lifetimes and session summaries, not roll-up ordering. Checked that raw retention alone would cover it: expired_raw has no roll-up input.

findings.title: The 'lose up to 5 seconds on power loss' promise is not backed by synchronous=NORMAL, and the phase 1 kill test cannot detect the shortfall
findings.evidence: raw.py:70 sets synchronous=NORMAL. https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html: 'A transaction committed in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL might roll back following a power loss or system crash. Transactions are durable across application crashes regardless of the synchronous setting or journal mode.' And: 'In WAL mode when synchronous is NORMAL (1), the WAL file is synchronized before each checkpoint ... but no sync operations occur during most transactions.' Probe wal_readers.py: 'log pages per tick: median 6 ... the log reached 3.9 MiB and was reset after 149 ticks'; strace: 'synchronous=normal: 20 fsync or fdatasync calls in 601 ticks ... log was synced about every 60 ticks'; 'synchronous=full: 621 ... about every 1 ticks'. crash_kill.py: 12 SIGKILLs, 'acknowledged ticks missing 0' each time.
findings.impact: docs/17-build-prompt.md:138 promises that 'a crash or power loss may lose up to 5 seconds'. On power loss or an OS crash, SQLite guarantees only the samples up to the last checkpoint: about 1 to 2.5 minutes at 1 s cadence, and longer at the idle cadence. The phase 1 gate kills the program (docs/15-phases-and-decisions.md:13), which by SQLite's own statement loses nothing whatever the setting, so the gate passes and the promise stays untested. No corruption risk: 'WAL mode is safe from corruption with synchronous=NORMAL'.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:138 and docs/16 R36: either (a) keep NORMAL and have the collector run PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE) every 5 s, which syncs the log and gives the bound, or (b) use synchronous=FULL for raw files, or (c) restate the promise: 'a program crash loses nothing committed; a power loss may lose the samples since the last checkpoint, up to N minutes'. Add a power-loss line to the gate wording, or say it is untested.
findings.cost: One sentence in the doc, and one timer line in the collector loop if (a).
findings.decision_question: Bound power-loss loss at 5 s with a checkpoint every 5 s (about 0.4 syncs a second), with synchronous=FULL (about 1 sync per tick), or relax the promise to 'since the last checkpoint'? Recommendation: a timed PASSIVE checkpoint every 5 s, measured in phase 1 for cost.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether the OS writeback makes 5 s true anyway. It might on some systems, but the brief rests the promise on SQLite and SQLite disclaims it. Checked R36: it states the promise and not the mechanism. The SIGKILL probe confirms that program crashes lose nothing, so only power loss and OS crashes are at issue.

findings.title: A program crash loses up to one keyframe interval of per-process CPU held in memory, so process rows stop adding up to workload rows
findings.evidence: raw.py:134-145: a process using less than 0.5% of a core never reaches 'pending >= self._cpu_share * waited' (both sides grow at the same rate), so its CPU stays in self._pending until a keyframe (every 600 s), an 8 MiB memory move or its exit. Probe crash_kill.py 12, 300 processes, SIGKILL: every trial 'integrity ok ... acknowledged ticks missing 0', but 'CPU held back in memory and lost with the process' was 47.27, 26.68, 56.16, ... 19.19 s per kill; 'process rows are short of the workload rows by 362.70 CPU-s over 12 kills' (1.14 CPU-s per tick, so one kill loses about 12 to 49 ticks' worth).
findings.impact: raw.py:5 and docs/14 claim 'sums stay exact'. After any collector crash, process-level sums (the process tree, and the hourly top-executables summary if built from process rows) undercount quiet processes by up to 10 minutes of their CPU. Workload totals are unaffected.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/raw.py:138: add 'or waited >= hold_limit_s' with hold_limit_s = 60, so held CPU is never older than a minute. The write threshold stays for busy processes. docs/14-baseline-modules.md store.raw: 'a crash loses at most 60 s of a quiet process's CPU from process rows; workload rows lose nothing committed'.
findings.cost: About 3 lines and one sentence. At 270 quiet processes it adds roughly 0.8 M rows per 48 h, about 10% of 8.1 M.
findings.refutation_attempt: Re-ran 12 trials: integrity was always ok and workload rows were complete, so only process rows are short. Checked whether close() flushing pending covers a crash: it runs only on a clean close (raw.py:227-232).

findings.title: A long-lived reader makes the write-ahead log grow without bound, and automatic checkpoints never truncate it, contrary to the brief
findings.evidence: Probe wal_readers.py: 'log size 4.0 MiB before; 110.1 MiB after an unfinished cursor was held across 4000 ticks (27 KiB a tick); 64.0 MiB 1500 ticks after the cursor closed (journal_size_limit is 64 MiB)'. raw.py:71 sets journal_size_limit=67108864. Truncation happens only in close() (raw.py:233). https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html: 'if there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.' docs/17-build-prompt.md:138: 'Keep read transactions short ... and truncate it at each checkpoint.'
findings.impact: The server's live view or WebSocket reads today's raw file continuously. One unexhausted cursor grows today's log by about 100 MB an hour, outside every budget figure. After it ends, the log stays at 64 MiB per open file instead of truncating. The disk budget is then off by up to 64 MiB per open raw, minute and history file.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:138: 'The writer runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) on a timer (combine it with the durability checkpoint); readers fetch all rows and end the read at once; disk_use counts the -wal files'. Optionally lower journal_size_limit to 4 MiB in raw.py:71.
findings.cost: One sentence and a one-line timer, with one pragma value changed.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether workload_samples could hold a cursor: it uses fetchall (raw.py:196-201), so the baseline reader is safe. The risk is in the readers still to be built, which the brief only asks to 'keep short'. A second-process read-only reader polled 40 times with 0 errors, so plain concurrent reading is fine.

findings.title: On Windows an open SQLite connection blocks deleting an expired file, and a retention pass that deletes only .db leaves side files and miscounts freed space
findings.evidence: SQLite Windows VFS, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sqlite/sqlite/master/src/os_win.c winOpen: 'dwShareMode = FILE_SHARE_READ | FILE_SHARE_WRITE;' (no FILE_SHARE_DELETE). https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-deletefilew: 'The DeleteFile function fails if an application attempts to delete a file that has other handles open for normal I/O or as a memory-mapped file (FILE_SHARE_DELETE must have been specified when other handles were opened).' and 'the file deletion does not occur until the last handle to the file is closed.' https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/c_fcntl_begin_atomic_write.html: the Windows VFS retries 'file read, file write, and file delete operations up to 10 times' for anti-virus, but only its own operations, not the os.remove that retention would call. Linux probe side_files.py: a mode=ro reader of a cleanly closed file leaves '2026-11-19.db-shm 32768 B, 2026-11-19.db-wal 0 B'; deleting the .db under an open reader leaves '2026-11-18.db-shm 32768 B, 2026-11-18.db-wal 0 B' behind. files.py:124 globs '*.db' while disk_use (files.py:154) counts '*.db*'.
findings.impact: Any open connection to an expired day blocks its deletion: the server's own query, the CLI, the dashboard, or a database browser the user left open. The phase 1 gate 'Deleting a day of raw data frees its space at once' (docs/15-phases-and-decisions.md:13) then fails under real use. Side files that retention never lists pile up and are counted against the budget forever. This settles item 4 of docs/reference/windows-priorities.md ('If it is, retention needs to retry later') from vendor source rather than leaving it open. Whether the -shm mapping also blocks deletion, and how anti-virus behaves, still needs a Windows run.
findings.proposed_change: docs/reference/windows-priorities.md item 4 and docs/17-build-prompt.md Store: 'Deletion is refused while any connection is open. Retention deletes the .db with its -wal and -shm, retries on the next pass, counts space as freed only when the files are gone, and the server opens closed files read-only and closes them after each query'. Make the P1 gate wording 'frees its space once no reader holds it'. src/submeter/store/files.py expired_raw and expired_minute: return the side files with each day.
findings.cost: Three sentences and about 6 lines in files.py.
findings.refutation_attempt: docs/reference/windows-priorities.md:60 already lists this as an unknown, so the finding narrows it rather than adding it. Checked whether SQLite's 'exclusive' URI path changes the share mode: it sets 0, which is stricter. The FILE_SHARE_DELETE quote is Microsoft's, and the share mode is from SQLite's source. The behaviour is not observed on Windows.
findings.would_confirm: On Windows: open a raw file with sqlite3.connect('file:...?mode=ro', uri=True), then os.remove() it from a second process and record the error; repeat with only the -shm present (the 'raw file on disk' line of scripts/platform_check.py).

findings.title: The baseline's only way to read a raw file writes to it, and anything that moves only the .db loses the data held in its write-ahead log
findings.evidence: raw.py:68-76: RawFile.__init__ opens read-write, sets journal_mode, runs CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and INSERTs into meta. raw.py:233: close() runs wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE). workload_samples exists only on RawFile. Probe schema_gaps.py part 4: 'RawFile on a day with no data created 2026-01-01.db (40960 B); RawFile has no way to open a file without writing to it'. side_files.py part 2: killed writer leaves '2026-11-20.db 4096 B ... -wal 3926392 B'; 'immutable=1 reader: fails with OperationalError: no such table: system_raw'; 'the .db alone, moved elsewhere: fails ... no such table'; 'mode=ro reader: reads 120 ticks'. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html: 'If a database file is separated from its WAL file, then transactions that were previously committed to the database might be lost, or the database file might become corrupted.'
findings.impact: A server that reads through RawFile becomes a second writer of the collector's files, which breaks 'every file has one writer' (docs/06-storage.md:9). It can also create a file for a day the collector never wrote. After a collector crash, yesterday's samples can live entirely in the -wal, and the collector never reopens yesterday's file. A quarantine ('Quarantine a damaged raw or minute file', docs/17-build-prompt.md:139), backup or copy that moves only the .db, or a reader opened with immutable=1, sees an empty day.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/raw.py: add a read-only opener (sqlite3.connect('file:PATH?mode=ro', uri=True), never immutable=1) that raises if the file is missing, and move workload_samples onto it. docs/17-build-prompt.md:139: 'quarantine moves the .db with its -wal and -shm'.
findings.cost: About 20 lines in raw.py, a test, and one clause in the doc.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether the brief already says readers open read-only. docs/17:112 says only 'Open closed files only for the length of a query'. Checked that a mode=ro reader works on a crashed file: it does on Linux (side_files part 2).

findings.title: The disk budget arithmetic omits the histograms, the number of series, 72 h of raw files and the non-raw files, mixes binary and decimal units, and its deletion order cannot enforce a 2 GB cap
findings.evidence: Probe row_sizes.py part C (real Buckets from roll_up, two 66-bin histograms, 12 of 132 bins filled on average): 'dense 8-byte floats, rowid table 1403 B a bucket; 9 series: 0.55 to 0.67 GB for 30 to 37 days; 26 series: 1.94 GB; 200 series: 14.95 GB'; 'one bucket as JSON is 891 B'; 'filled bins only, plus 18 catalogue fields 311 B a bucket; ... 200 series: 3.31 GB'; brief: 250 B. Part B: per-core rows 16 cores '2.76 M rows and 85 MB per 48 h', not in the arithmetic. retention_calendar.py part 3: 'at 9.00 h UTC: 3 files hold 57.0 h; delete one -> 33.0 h; delete two -> 9.0 h, which is under the 24-hour floor'; docs/08 'raw retention about 13 h' contradicts the floor. budget_arithmetic.py: every docs/08 row recomputes, but the formula uses 48 h of raw while up to 72 h sit on disk (part 2: 1.10 GB at 72 h), and ignores about 0.55 GB of other files. For the 500 ms row ('Active only') that is 1.32 x 1.5 + 0.55 = 2.53 GB. units.py:31-34,56: 'Units are binary, so 1 GB is 1024**3 bytes', while docs figures are rows x bytes / 1e9. docs/17-build-prompt.md:141: budget deletes raw, then backups, then raises a finding; minute files and history are never deleted. docs/04-features.md:22: 'a 2 GB cap that is enforced exactly'.
findings.impact: The minute tier can be 5 to 6 times its 0.1 GB estimate with the obvious encoding. With many workloads (doctor only warns at 200 names), minute and history files alone can exceed the budget, and the deletion order then has nothing left to delete. The docs/08 status column calls a setting in budget when its peak on-disk total is over it.
findings.proposed_change: docs/06-storage.md 'Disk use after a year': state the bucket encoding (sparse histogram bins in one blob, about 300 B a bucket), give the figure per series and at 200 series, and include per-core rows. docs/08-configuration.md:24-25,38: compute disk at 72 h of raw plus the other files, and replace 'about N hours' with 'raw drops to 24 to 48 h; below the 24 h floor a finding is raised'. Either state that GB means 1024^3 or make parse_size decimal. docs/17-build-prompt.md:141 and docs/04:22: add minute files to the deletion order or drop 'enforced exactly'.
findings.cost: About 10 changed lines across four docs.
findings.decision_question: When raw is at its 24 h floor and backups are down to one and the store is still over budget, should the oldest minute files be deleted (down to, say, 7 days), or is the budget a warning only? Recommendation: delete minute files oldest first down to 7 days, then raise a finding, and keep history.
findings.refutation_attempt: Recomputed every docs/08 and docs/06 figure: all match their own formulas (budget_arithmetic.py parts 1 to 3), so the issue is what the formulas leave out, not the arithmetic. The raw bytes per row are conservative (measured 48 B synthetic and 59 B for real sample rows, against 90 B), so raw is not the problem. The docs/03 store status sample adds up (1192 MB shown as 1.19 GB).

findings.title: The stored schema cannot hold several metrics the catalogue promises, and its version rule breaks on the first mid-day upgrade
findings.evidence: raw.py:41-52 and models.py:135-175: workload_raw and Bucket carry one memory_bytes, while the catalogue (docs/06-storage.md:82-83) needs two memory metrics (private bytes or RSS plus swap for growth, and USS or PSS with the age of the reading for totals). process_raw has no I/O or handle columns, though docs/06-storage.md:120 says Submeter 'records bytes read and written, and handle counts, per process'. There is no per-core table (docs/06:90). SampleBatch drops memory_total_bytes (models.py:122-131), so buckets cannot record memory capacity (docs/17-build-prompt.md:121). rules.py:208-209 turn unavailable I/O into 0 (schema_gaps.py part 2: 'io_read_bytes None is totalled into a workload row with io_read_bytes = 0'). Probe schema_gaps.py part 3: 'a version 2 collector reopened the version 1 file without an error. The file still says schema_version 1 ... Its 11-value insert then fails' (raw.py:72-76 CREATE IF NOT EXISTS plus INSERT OR IGNORE). files.py:126-128 skip any raw name that is not an ISO date, so a second file for the same day would never expire.
findings.impact: An upgrade during the day crashes the collector on every write until UTC midnight. Each missing metric means a later schema change. Minute files live up to 37 days, so two changes inside that window leave files that 'readers accept the current and previous versions' (docs/17-build-prompt.md:140) cannot read. Unreadable I/O shows as zero instead of unavailable (docs/08-configuration.md:126).
findings.proposed_change: Plan: put every catalogue column into schema version 1 of the raw, minute and history tables now, nullable, with NULL meaning unavailable. That covers both memory metrics, per-process I/O and handles, memory capacity, and a per-core table. aggregate keeps None when any part is unknown. Fix now: docs/17-build-prompt.md:140 should read 'readers accept every version still on disk'. raw.py: on opening a file whose schema_version differs, start a new file for the rest of the day under a name files.py understands, and teach expired_raw that name.
findings.cost: About 10 lines and two doc sentences now. The schema additions are a task in phase 1.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked the table list: it matches docs/13 exactly (schema_gaps part 1), so the gap is columns, not tables. Checked whether 'a closed day's file is never migrated' covers the open file: it does not. Today's file is open when an upgrade lands.

findings.title: Buckets that span an epoch or capacity change carry only the latest epoch and core count, and whether adaptive cadence starts epochs is unstated
findings.evidence: rollup.py:105,118 apply one epoch and one logical_cores to the whole roll_up call. rollup.py:158-159 merge keeps latest.logical_cores and latest.epoch. Probe merge_capacity.py: '60 minute buckets: epochs [3, 4], logical cores [8, 16], CPU 43200 s of 43200 core-seconds of capacity: 100% busy'; 'the merged hour keeps epoch 4 and logical_cores 16 ... = 75%'. docs/06-storage.md:98: an epoch is a stretch in which 'the sampling intervals ... stayed the same'. docs/08-configuration.md:60: adaptive mode 'moves between the active and idle intervals'. Neither doc says whether such a switch is an epoch.
findings.impact: Percentages for an hour or day that spans a hardware change are wrong (75% against a true 100%). This breaks 'Percentages use the capacity recorded in each bucket' (docs/06:101). A bucket that mixes epochs looks like one epoch, so 'a comparison that crosses an interval change is flagged' cannot see it. If adaptive switches count as epochs, nearly every hour spans several. If they do not, buckets mix 1 s and 5 s maxima with no record.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/rollup.py: key accumulators by (start, series, epoch) and make merge refuse mixed epochs, or store first and last epoch and minimum and maximum logical cores, and compute capacity as the sum over the source buckets of covered_s x logical_cores. docs/06-storage.md:98: 'adaptive switches between the configured active and idle intervals are not epochs; each bucket records the shortest and longest interval it contains'.
findings.cost: About 10 lines in rollup.py and two fields on Bucket, plus one doc sentence.
findings.decision_question: Does an adaptive-cadence switch start an epoch? Recommendation: no. Epochs track configuration, and each bucket stores its minimum and maximum interval_s so maxima and percentiles can be flagged per bucket.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether the server could cut buckets at epoch edges anyway: roll_up offers no way to do so, and merge accepts mixed buckets without complaint. A core-count change is rare (VM resize, hot-plug); interval changes are not.

findings.title: Local days use one fixed UTC offset across daylight saving, cannot be cut from hourly buckets in half-hour zones, and Windows has no time zone database without tzdata
findings.evidence: growth.py:102-110: daily_minimums(utc_offset_s) applies one offset to every timestamp. Probe local_days.py: 'New York, asked on 20 November (UTC-5): of 336 hourly buckets from 25 October to 7 November, 8 fall in a different local day under the fixed offset ... a nightly low at 00:00 to 01:00 local time is present in every true local day; with the fixed offset these days have no low at all: ['2026-11-01']'; 'Kolkata (UTC+5.5): 3 of 72 hourly buckets hold parts of two local days'; '15 zone names ... not a whole number of hours from UTC today'; 'tzdata package is installed: False'. https://docs.python.org/3/library/zoneinfo.html: 'Some systems, including notably Windows systems, do not have an IANA database available, and so for projects targeting cross-platform compatibility that require time zone data, it is recommended to declare a dependency on tzdata.' pyproject.toml dependencies: pydantic, psutil, typer only.
findings.impact: R35's fix ('days are worked out in your time zone when you ask') is not what the baseline does. The slow-growth check (R34: daily minimum over 7 to 90 days) puts an hour of data in the wrong day at every daylight-saving change and can lose a day's low. In half-hour zones, local daily totals from the hourly tier are off by up to 30 minutes at each end. A zone-aware fix will fail on Windows without tzdata.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/analysis/growth.py daily_minimums: take a tzinfo (ZoneInfo or the local zone) and compute the offset per timestamp. pyproject.toml: add 'tzdata; sys_platform == "win32"'. docs/06-storage.md:103: 'in zones not a whole number of hours from UTC, days within 30 days come from minute buckets; older days from hourly buckets are approximate by up to 30 minutes'.
findings.cost: About 5 lines in growth.py, one dependency line, one doc sentence and a test.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked the tests and docs for a per-timestamp zone rule: docs/06:103 and 17:132 state the intent; only growth.py implements it, with a fixed offset. Confirmed the Windows tzdata point from docs.python.org rather than from memory.

nothing_found: ISO-week file names: 4383 days from 2024 to 2035 each map to a week file whose Monday-to-Sunday span holds them, the names sort in time order, and 2026 and 2032 get a W53 (retention_calendar.py part 1). 2027-01-03 maps to 2026-W53.db, as it should.

Whole-day and whole-week expiry: with checks every hour for 70 days, 3 raw files spanning 48 to 71 h and 5 to 6 minute files spanning 30 to 37 days, matching docs/06 '2 to 3 daily files' and '5 to 6 weekly files'.
SIGKILL during writes: 12 of 12 trials 'integrity ok' and 0 acknowledged ticks missing from workload rows. The one-transaction-per-tick commit holds; only held per-process CPU is lost (reported).
A read-only reader in a second process while the writer runs: 40 polls, 0 errors, counts rising throughout.
Closing order: once a read-write connection opens and closes the file, the -wal and -shm are removed. Only read-only last closers leave them.
Recreating a deleted .db beside a stale -wal: integrity ok, and the stale log was not applied (side_files.py part 2).
docs/08 results table: all 11 rows recompute exactly from the printed formulas; docs/06 disk table and docs/05 daily volumes recompute too (budget_arithmetic.py parts 1 to 3).
docs/03 store status sample: the 11 sizes add to 1192 MB, shown as 1.19 GB, and the expiry notes are consistent with 09:00 UTC on 20 November.

Raw bytes per row: 48 B synthetic and 59 B for real sample rows (process_raw 48 B, workload_raw 80 B), against 90 B assumed, so the raw estimate is conservative. In a 2-minute real file 66% of bytes are per-day tables, and the command text is stored twice, in the table and in its UNIQUE index (raw_tables_real.py).
Raw table list in raw.py matches docs/13 exactly.
Rollup merge keeps sums, extremes and histograms exact when buckets are filled one accumulator per window (bucket_membership approach C: +0.00% in all four cases).

measurements: Gap: minute bucket covered_s 3601 of 60; hour 09:00 covered 4201 s (600 s observed), p50 0.006 against a true 2.0 cores; system busy share 12.5% against 50%. Bucket membership, CPU kept by method A, B, C: 1 s at phase 0.37: -1.67%, -96.72%, 0%. 1 s at phase 0.63: 0, 0, 0. 5 s: -8.33%, -90.28%, 0. 10 s: -16.67%, -82.22%, 0. Long intervals over 30 s: CPU kept 0%. Samples of 120 s and 600 s: covered_s 120 and 600 of 60, written up to 59 and 299 s after the bucket ended. Clock steps: back 30 s lost 30 of 120 CPU-s; back 50 s across midnight lost 50 of 120 and reopened the closed day; back 1 h left 4200 s between keyframes. SIGKILL x12: integrity ok in all, 0 acknowledged ticks lost, 13.1 to 56.2 CPU-s of process rows lost per kill (362.7 in total). WAL: 6 pages a tick median, 30 on a keyframe tick; reset after 149 ticks; NORMAL gave 20 syncs in 601 ticks (log about every 60), FULL gave 621; a held cursor grew the log to 110.1 MiB in 4000 ticks (27 KiB a tick), and it stayed at 64 MiB afterwards. Side files: a mode=ro read leaves -shm 32768 B and -wal 0 B; a killed writer leaves .db 4096 B and -wal 3.9 MB. Rows: process_raw 47-48 B, workload_raw 57 B synthetic and 80 B real, system_raw 30 B synthetic and 102 B real. Buckets: 1403 B dense rowid, 891 B JSON, 311 B sparse plus catalogue fields; brief assumes 250 B. Minute tier with 9 series: 0.55-0.67 GB dense, 0.12-0.15 GB sparse. With 200 series: 14.95 GB dense, 3.31 GB sparse. Per-core rows at 16 cores: 85 MB per 48 h. parse_size('2GB') = 2,147,483,648 bytes. Daylight saving, New York: 8 of 336 hourly buckets in the wrong day. Kolkata: 1 hourly bucket a day straddles local midnight. tzdata not installed.
